items.prompt: Identify whether production within an economy is the domestic or national boundary test.
items.canonical_answer: Domestic (1).

items.prompt: Explain the difference between GDP and GNP.
items.canonical_answer: GDP concerns domestic production (1), whereas GNP adjusts it for net primary income from abroad (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: domestic boundary versus net-income adjustment, 1 each.

items.prompt: Explain the GNP result when GDP is N$500 million, relevant income from abroad N$30 million and paid abroad N$45 million.
items.canonical_answer: Net income is minus N$15 million (1), so GNP is N$485 million on the stated basis, below GDP because payments exceed receipts (1).
marking_guidance: Context: flows; reasoning: net sign 1; result: correct adjustment 1.

items.prompt: Explain why relevant income paid abroad can make GNP below GDP rather than being ignored because production is domestic.
items.canonical_answer: GDP counts the production within the economy (1), while the net-income adjustment subtracts excess payments over receipts, so national product can be lower (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: domestic production versus income flow; boundary/test: location plus net adjustment, 1 each.

items.prompt: Explain why output and expenditure methods are not two extra totals to add together.
items.canonical_answer: They examine production and final spending on the same activity (1), so adding their whole totals would repeatedly count that activity rather than create new output (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: different views, not additive separate production, 1 each.

items.prompt: Explain why adding N$60 input sales, N$100 processed-output sales and N$160 final sales overcounts the simplified chain.
items.canonical_answer: The earlier input values are embodied in later sales (1), so adding all 320 repeats them; value added 60+40+60 gives 160 (1).

items.prompt: Define a real national-income measure.
items.canonical_answer: A monetary aggregate adjusted for price changes to support comparison of production over time.
marking_guidance: Meaning: price-adjusted aggregate 1; qualifier: real production comparison 1.

items.prompt: Explain how real national-income measurement can support economic-policy assessment.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: comparable output data are measured over time (1); the price adjustment helps separate real production change from higher nominal prices, informing decisions (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change: measurement 1; mechanism/effect: price-comparable output informs policy 1.

items.prompt: Explain why higher total real output alone does not prove better living standards for every resident.
items.canonical_answer: Population and distribution can change (1), while external costs or omitted outcomes may offset gains, so the aggregate is not an individual welfare measure (1).
marking_guidance: Context: real total; reasoning: population/distribution 1; result: limited welfare conclusion 1.

items.prompt: Define Gross Domestic Product.
items.canonical_answer: The value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a stated period.
marking_guidance: Meaning: The value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a stated period. Distinguishing feature: the specified boundary or accounting route. Award 1 for core meaning and 1 for precise qualifier.

items.prompt: Define Gross National Product.
items.canonical_answer: The total value of final goods and services produced by a country’s residents and their firms, at home or abroad, in a year; GNP = GDP + income from abroad − income paid abroad.
marking_guidance: Meaning: value of output produced by a country’s residents in a year (1). Distinguishing feature: GDP plus income received from abroad minus income paid abroad (1).

items.prompt: Define National Income.
items.canonical_answer: The total income earned by a country’s factors of production (wages, rent, interest and profit) in a year; on the conventional factor-cost basis it equals GNP at factor cost minus depreciation.
marking_guidance: Meaning: total income earned by the factors of production in a year (1). Distinguishing feature: equals GNP minus depreciation (1).

items.prompt: Define the output method.
items.canonical_answer: Adding value added in productive activities, avoiding repeated counting of intermediate inputs.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Adding value added in productive activities, avoiding repeated counting of intermediate inputs. Distinguishing feature: the specified boundary or accounting route. Award 1 for core meaning and 1 for precise qualifier.

items.prompt: Define the income method.
items.canonical_answer: Adding all incomes earned from production (wages, rent, interest and profit), excluding transfer payments such as pensions and grants.
marking_guidance: Meaning: adding incomes earned from production (1). Distinguishing feature: wages, rent, interest and profit, excluding transfer payments (1).

items.prompt: Define the expenditure method.
items.canonical_answer: Adding all final spending on the country’s output: consumer spending + investment + government spending + (exports − imports).

items.prompt: An economy reports GDP N$800 million, relevant primary income received abroad N$50 million and paid abroad N$35 million. Money-value GDP rises over time but no output-price index or population change is supplied. (a) Describe three accounting features (6). (b) Examine what can be concluded about national product and real performance (7). (c) Suggest evidence needed for a wider comparison (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) GDP concerns production within the economy. Net primary income is positive N$15 million. GNP is therefore N$815 million on the stated basis. (b) The income adjustment differs from trade flows and raises GNP above GDP here. A money-value rise does not isolate real output change because prices may rise. Missing population and distribution data limit per-person or welfare claims. (c) Obtain consistent real measures with a relevant price basis, population and distribution information, plus evidence about omitted outcomes and external costs. Keep the accounting boundary fixed across periods. The judgement should recognise the calculable national adjustment while withholding unsupported real-growth or welfare conclusions.
marking_guidance: Context: economy. Parts/allocation: (a) boundary, net flow, adjusted total 2 each=6. (b) adjustment mechanism 2, real/nominal 3, wider limits 2=7. (c) comparable data 3, wider evidence 2, conditional judgement 2=7. Mechanism: consistent accounting links production and income; judgement requires comparable wider evidence.

items.prompt: (a) Define GDP (2). (b) Define GNP (2). (c) Explain why wealth differs from a period’s production (2). (d) Explain value added (2). (e) Explain why transfers are not additional factor income merely on receipt (2). (f) Explain why imports are adjusted out of domestic expenditure (2). (g) Explain why nominal growth needs a price check (2). (h) Explain one limit of aggregate income as welfare evidence (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Final goods/services value produced domestically in a period. (b) Domestic product plus net primary income abroad. (c) Wealth is accumulated stock; production is a period flow. (d) Output value less intermediate inputs, avoiding repeated counting. (e) Redistribution does not create new production income. (f) The production occurs abroad, so the domestic boundary excludes it. (g) Higher current-money value may reflect prices. (h) Distribution or external costs can differ from the average total.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2. (a/b) boundary plus adjustment/period; (c) stock/flow; (d) subtraction plus double-count reason; (e) receipt versus generation; (f) location plus exclusion; (g) prices versus real output; (h) named limit plus implication.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
items.reviewed_unchanged: Re-read after step-6 revision of CL-6145-7.3-09; this text needed no change.

items.prompt: A chain has a grower selling N$60 output with no purchased intermediate inputs, a processor selling N$100 after buying that N$60 input, and a final producer selling N$160 after buying the N$100 processed input. All final goods are purchased. Relevant factor incomes on the same simplified basis total N$160. (a) Define the output method (2). (b) Explain the value-added total (4). (c) Explain how the income and expenditure routes relate to it (7). (d) Discuss whether these matching totals prove high living standards (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Adding value added across production activities without intermediate double counting. (b) Grower 60, processor 40 and final producer 60 sum 160. Adding all sales 320 repeats inputs. (c) Factor incomes generated by this production total 160 under the given consistent basis. Final expenditure is 160 because all stated final goods are purchased and no other adjustments occur in the illustration. The methods view the same activity, not three totals to sum. (d) Reconciliation supports the simplified accounting, but the size has no population, distribution, price-comparison or external-cost context. A correct total is useful evidence of activity, not proof of welfare. Assess the relevant wider outcomes before judging living standards.
marking_guidance: Context: chain. Parts/allocation: (a) value-added route 1, avoiding repeats 1. (b) correct stage additions 2, total/double-count explanation 2=4. (c) income mechanism 2, expenditure route 3, same-activity distinction 2=7. (d) measurement benefit 2, welfare limits 2, supported judgement 3=7. Mechanism: consistent accounting links production and income; judgement requires comparable wider evidence.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an analyst should rank two economies’ welfare solely by unadjusted money-value GDP totals when population, prices, distribution and environmental effects differ (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: GDP provides a defined measure of domestic production and can indicate the scale of resources generated. Against: raw money totals can reflect different prices and population, while distribution and external costs affect lived outcomes. Definitions and coverage may also differ. Judgement: use comparable real and per-person measures alongside distribution and wider evidence. The condition for a welfare ranking is a relevant common basis and information about the outcomes beyond aggregate production; the raw totals alone are insufficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for: defined production information up to 4. Argument against: comparability/welfare limits up to 4. Judgement: distinct common-basis and wider-outcome condition 1. Total 9. Condition: common real/population basis and welfare evidence must support ranking.
